title: Out of the stone pillar
hook: a boon with every loophole closed, and a god who steps out of stone
carry: the Lord shows up to keep his devotee's word
tomorrow: the lion won't calm down. who dares walk up to him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord lives in every being's story began with Prahlada, the boy who told the demon children the Lord lives in everyone. His father pointed at a pillar: is he in this?

A phone contract or a lease comes with pages of fine print, written so the company is covered whatever happens. Hiranyakashipu wrote fine print with a god. Long before this night, after fierce austerities, he won a boon from Brahma, and he closed every loophole he could think of. Now, in the hall, the king strikes the pillar with his fist. It splits open with a roar, and out steps something his list had no box for.
screen: `FINE PRINT THAT COVERS EVERYTHING.` → `A BOON WITH NO LOOPHOLES.` → `THE PILLAR SPLITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the fine print, as the Bhagavata Purana gives it. No death from any being Brahma created. Not by a human, not by an animal. Not inside, not outside. Not by day, not by night. Not on the ground, not in the sky. Not by any weapon. Brahma grants it all. Now look at what steps out of the pillar. Narasimha: a body like a man's, a head like a lion's. Not a human, not an animal, and not made by Brahma. He carries the king to the threshold of the hall, neither inside nor outside. The sun is going down: twilight. He lays the king across his lap, neither ground nor sky. No weapon, only claws. Every word of the boon is kept. But the Bhagavata stops to say why he came this way, and that's the teaching. He came to make his devotee's words true, and to show that he is present in every being. Prahlada had said the Lord is everywhere. The king picked the plainest, deadest thing in the room, a stone pillar, and the Lord was in that too. This is the heart of what Hindus mean when they say God is everywhere: not only in the temple, but in stone, in an animal, in the person you'd least expect. And it's why Narasimha is the form so many families call on for protection: the Lord who keeps his word to the one who trusts him.
screen: `THE FINE PRINT: EVERY LOCK.` · `NOT MAN, NOT BEAST.` · `THE DOORWAY, THE DUSK, THE LAP.` · `TO MAKE HIS DEVOTEE'S WORD TRUE.` · then, large: `EVEN IN A STONE PILLAR.`

segments.voice: Some families pray to Narasimha for protection. If you pray, say quietly, a few times: om namo bhagavate narasimhaya, I bow to the Lord, Narasimha. If you don't, rest a hand on something solid near you, a wall, a table, a doorframe, and hold the story's claim for a few slow breaths: not even this is empty.
Narasimha: the man-lion, who stepped out of a pillar to make a child's word true, and ended it at dusk.
For the road: the Lord shows up to keep his devotee's word. Even a stone pillar wasn't empty. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindus keep Narasimha Jayanti at dusk, the hour of the story, and temple images sometimes show the moment in the doorway, the king across the man-lion's lap.

fork.setup: a friend sees a picture of Narasimha bursting out of a pillar and asks why Hindus tell it that way. what does the story answer?
options: to show the Lord is in everything, even stone, and keeps his devotee's word.
to show a god can always find a loophole in a deal.
because Vishnu happened to live inside that one pillar.
fork.reveal: Prahlada said the Lord is everywhere. the king picked a stone pillar, and the Lord came out of it to prove the boy right.

original.note: Sanskrit: twilight, the joining of day and night. Narasimha came at that hour.

chat.says: Rohan saw the Narasimha painting at Nani's and wants the hall light on all night. how do i explain claws??
options: tell it the way the story goes: the lion came out to protect a kid who trusted him.
say the lion is only angry at kids who misbehave, so he's fine.
tell him it's only a painting, and quickly change the subject.
chat.meaning: Narasimha stepped out of the pillar to make Prahlada's word true and protect him. For a scared kid, start with who the lion protects.

tie.story: Hiranyakashipu struck the pillar, and Narasimha stepped out of it to protect Prahlada and prove him right.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Rohan the lion in Nani's picture is the one who protects kids who trust him.
tie.you: where's the last place you'd expect to find the holy?

notes: Puzzle shape: the strange detail is a boon with every loophole closed; solved clause by clause. No count of the boon's conditions is stated.

Confirm in Bhagavata 7.3.35–38 the conditions (no being created by Brahma; not human or animal; not inside or outside; not by day or night; not on the ground or in the sky; no weapon) and in 7.8 the matching end (the threshold of the assembly hall, at evening twilight, on his thighs, with his nails). Paraphrased.
For parents: the king's death is told without gore ('no weapon at all, only his claws'); the chat gives a sentence a parent or older cousin could say to a scared child.
sandhya as the joining of day and night (original game): confirm under the claims rule.
Surprising fact: every condition of the boon is kept word for word; the answer comes through the in-between.
